common_name: New Hampshire Midget Watermelon (Ultra-Compact Short-Season Icebox Watermelon)

planting.note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed to at least 70°F, or start indoors 3 weeks early in short-season areas.

directions: Bred at the University of New Hampshire and released in 1951, this is one of the earliest true short-vine watermelons ever developed, making it a workhorse for northern gardeners and anyone with a short frost-free window. Vines stay compact enough for a large container or a small raised bed, and the round 4-6 pound fruits with pale flesh mature fast rather than for exceptional sweetness. Keep soil evenly moist through fruit set, then ease off watering as the melons near ripeness to concentrate what sugar they do develop. Its main value is reliability where longer-season Southern varieties simply run out of summer.
sources: University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension

planting.note: Direct sow in hills 1-2 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed, or transplant 3-week-old seedlings to avoid disturbing the taproot.

directions: Tiger Baby gets its name from the dark gray-green rind striped with bold tiger-like markings, wrapped around a compact 7-8 pound icebox-size fruit with sweet, crisp red flesh. Its shorter maturity window compared to full-size Southern heirlooms makes it a good pick for gardeners north of the traditional watermelon belt who still want a full-flavored melon. Fertilize modestly since excess nitrogen favors vine growth over fruiting, and thump or check the ground spot for creamy yellowing to judge ripeness. The single-serving size makes it easy to chill whole and slice fresh without leftovers going to waste.

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after soil has warmed past 70°F; space hills generously since vines are vigorous and disease-tolerant enough to be grown in humid climates without heavy spray programs.

directions: Released in 1965 from the LSU AgCenter's Calhoun Research Station as a cross involving Calhoun Sweet and Charleston Gray, this variety was bred specifically to bring stronger disease resistance to the classic gray-rind Southern watermelon type. It produces 25-30 pound oblong fruits with light gray-green rind and sweet red flesh, and it holds up better against fungal wilts than its Charleston Gray parent, letting it succeed as far north as Massachusetts with proper season length. Give it full sun, warm fertile soil, and steady moisture through fruit development, then withhold water as fruits near maturity. It's a solid choice for gardeners who want old-style picnic-watermelon size and flavor with fewer disease headaches than older heirlooms.

common_name: Yellow Baby Watermelon (AAS-Winning Yellow-Fleshed Icebox Watermelon)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost once soil is reliably warm; this fast-maturing hybrid rewards an early start under black plastic mulch in cooler regions.

directions: An All-America Selections winner from the 1970s, Yellow Baby was one of the first widely available yellow-fleshed watermelons bred for home gardens, packing bright lemon-yellow flesh and thin, tender rind into a round 7-pound icebox-size fruit. The novel flesh color and honeyed flavor make it a conversation piece at the table, and its fast maturity suits shorter growing seasons better than full-size Southern types. Grow it exactly as you would any bush-type icebox watermelon: full sun, consistent moisture until fruit begins to ripen, then reduced watering to concentrate sugars. Because the pale flesh makes the usual red-ripeness cues useless, rely on the drying tendril and yellowing ground spot to judge harvest timing.

common_name: Crimson Tide Watermelon (Fusarium-Resistant Crimson Sweet Type Hybrid)

planting.note: Direct sow in warm, well-drained soil after last frost, or transplant young seedlings; this hybrid's Fusarium wilt resistance makes it a dependable choice for fields or beds with a history of vine decline.

directions: Crimson Tide is a Crimson Sweet-type F1 hybrid bred for growers who need reliable Fusarium wilt resistance without giving up the classic bright red, crisp-fleshed eating quality that made Crimson Sweet famous. Fruits run large, around 20-25 pounds, semi-elongated in shape, with a slightly darker green stripe pattern than standard Crimson Sweet. Because seed-borne and soil-borne wilts can build up in beds planted to melons repeatedly, this hybrid is a practical option for gardeners rotating crops on limited space where full rotation isn't always possible. Manage it like any full-size vining watermelon: full sun, warm soil, steady moisture through fruit fill, and a dry-down period before harvest to maximize sweetness.

common_name: Sweet Beauty Watermelon (AAS-Winning High-Brix Icebox Watermelon)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed, or start indoors 3 weeks ahead for an earlier harvest; this variety was recognized by All-America Selections judges specifically for its eating quality.

directions: Sweet Beauty is a small-space, single-serving icebox watermelon that won an All-America Selections award for consistently outscoring other compact varieties in sugar content during trials, with recorded Brix readings above 11. Fruits are oblong, 5-7 pounds, with dark green rind and medium green stripes and dense, sweet red flesh, and the vines stay manageable at roughly 8-10 feet, making the variety a good fit for smaller vegetable gardens. Grow it with full sun and even moisture through fruit development, then cut back watering as fruits ripen to keep the sugar concentration high. Its combination of compact vine habit and top-tier flavor makes it an easy choice for gardeners who don't have room for sprawling full-size Southern types but still want genuinely sweet, crisp melon.
